answers.1: Three machines: the client, the edge server (CDN, default 300 km from the client) and the origin server (default 6,000 km from the edge). There are two distances: client–edge (the 'short path') and edge–origin (the 'long path'). Other entities: round trips (TCP handshake, TLS 1.3 handshake, the request), the edge cache with its hits, misses and TTL, processing time (1 ms at the edge, 20 ms at the origin), and the edge's open connection to the origin.
answers.2: With no CDN, the client talks to the origin directly. The model takes that distance to be the edge–origin distance. With a CDN, the client does its handshakes and sends its request to the edge. On a hit, the edge answers from its cache. On a miss, the edge sends one round trip to the origin over a connection it keeps open, caches the answer for its TTL (set by Cache-Control: max-age), and replies. Each round trip costs about 1 ms per 100 km of distance.
answers.3: A new HTTPS request needs 3 round trips, and each costs time in proportion to distance. A CDN moves all 3 onto the short client–edge path, so the long path is paid at most once (on a miss) instead of three times.
answers.4: The key variable is the distance. As the edge–origin (= client–origin) distance grows, the no-CDN time grows by 3 × its RTT, the miss time grows by only 1 × that RTT, and the hit time does not change. So the CDN's advantage grows. As the client–edge distance grows, both CDN rows grow by 3 × the short RTT. Once the edge is about as far as the origin, the gain disappears or turns into a loss.
answers.5: Assumption: straight-line paths, a new connection for every request, and an origin that is as far from the client as it is from the edge. Fact: light in fiber travels at about two thirds of its vacuum speed, so 100 km of fiber costs about 1 ms per round trip.
answers.6: Before the first response byte, a new HTTPS request spends 3 round trips (TCP, TLS 1.3, request), and each costs about 1 ms per 100 km. Without a CDN, all three cross the long distance to the origin: 3 × 60 + 20 = 200 ms at 6,000 km. A CDN terminates those round trips at a nearby edge (3 × 3 ms at 300 km). A hit then costs about 10 ms. A miss adds one long round trip over an already-open edge–origin connection plus processing, about 90 ms. The gain shrinks as the edge's distance approaches the origin's distance, and the model ignores connection reuse, DNS, bandwidth and real routing.
answers.7: The miss and hit totals were hardest. The page writes out the formula only for no CDN (the Level 3 'law'), so I had to rebuild the miss (3×short + long + 1 + 20 = 90) and hit (3×short + 1 = 10) formulas from the script. The geometry was also confusing. The diagram puts the edge between client and origin (which would make client–origin 6,300 km), but the model says client–origin equals edge–origin. Writing all three formulas next to each other and stating the geometry plainly in the diagram would help.
answers.8: About 200 ms. That is 3 round trips (TCP, TLS 1.3, request) × 60 ms (6,000 km at 1 ms per 100 km) = 180 ms, plus 20 ms of origin processing. Most of the time is distance, paid three times.
answers.9: With a CDN, the 3 round trips of a new connection go over the short path (3 × 3 ms at the defaults). The miss then adds only one long round trip (60 ms), because the edge reuses an open connection to the origin with no new handshakes. Without a CDN, the client pays the long round trip 3 times (180 ms). So the miss takes about 90 ms against 200 ms.
answers.10: The page's verdict says the gain is small when the edge is not much closer than the origin; the script's threshold is client–edge > edge–origin / 3. The limits section adds cases where the model overstates the gain: a request on an already-open connection (keep-alive, HTTP/2) needs only 1 round trip, TLS resumption saves a round trip, and large files depend on bandwidth. Per-user responses (such as account pages) are always misses, so they never get the hit benefit.
answers.11: The summary only says that a miss is faster 'as long as the edge is much closer than the origin', and the verdict text says 'the edge is not closer than the origin'. From the script's formulas, a miss is slower when 3×short + 21 > 3×long + 20, that is, when 3×short + 1 > 2×long. So a miss is already slower once the client–edge distance is more than about two thirds of the origin distance (e.g., edge 2,000 km, origin 1,000 km: 91 ms vs 50 ms). The page never states this threshold.

terms: The edge machine is called 'edge' (SVG, Level 1), 'edge server' (lede, Level 2 step 1) and 'CDN' in row names ('CDN · cache miss').
The miss case is called 'cache miss' (lede, SVG 'only on a cache miss', row label) and 'miss' (instrument text, summary item 3).
The client–edge path is called 'short path' (lede, Level 2, Level 3, summary), 'short' (SVG label), 'Client to edge' (slider label) and 'nearby edge' (lede, summary).
The handshake round trips are called 'TCP + TLS handshakes' (legend), 'handshakes' (instrument text), 'a new connection' (predict text, limits card) and 'TCP and TLS' (Level 2 step 2).

The end point of the timing is called 'before the first byte arrives' (lede), 'from the first packet to the response' (predict question) and 'answer' (predict text: 'The origin takes about 20 ms to answer').
The origin's 20 ms is called 'to answer' (predict section), 'processing' (legend) and 'processing times' (limits card).
The limits card 'A new connection for each request' is labelled 'simplification' but carries the CSS class 'assumption', so the same tag means two things.
unexplained: Level 4 verdict, the '×' ratio ('A hit is 20× faster than no CDN'). It is shown with 0 or 1 decimal depending on size, and the page never says what ratio would count as a meaningful gain.
The slider ranges 50–2,000 km and 500–15,000 km are shown with no indication of what typical real edge or origin distances are.
The verdict 'the gain is small' fires when client–edge > edge–origin / 3. The '/3' threshold is never stated or explained.
'Edge processing 1 ms' appears only in the limits card and in the script. The visible stacked bar adds 1 + 20 = 21 ms of processing on a miss without saying that the 21 is edge plus origin.
Default results (90 ms miss, 10 ms hit) are never stated in the text. The reader must read them off the bars.
missing_why: 'A new connection needs 3 round trips (TCP, TLS 1.3, then the request itself)' (predict section). The page never says why TCP and TLS 1.3 each cost exactly one round trip.
'Light in fiber goes 100 km and back in about 1 ms' (predict section). The fact card gives two thirds of vacuum speed but never shows the arithmetic (200,000 km/s → 0.5 ms each way per 100 km).
Level 3 'law': 'no CDN ≈ 3 × RTT + 20 ms'. No matching formula is shown for the miss (3×short + long + edge + origin processing) or the hit (3×short + edge processing).

'The edge asks the origin over a connection it keeps open' (instrument text, Level 2 step 4). The page does not say why the edge can keep that connection open when the client cannot, which is the step the whole miss result rests on.
Summary item 3, 'as long as the edge is much closer than the origin'. The condition is never derived (by the formulas, a miss is slower once 3×short + 1 > 2×long).

Verdict text 'The edge is not closer than the origin here, so the CDN adds distance' fires whenever the miss is slower. By the formulas that already happens when the edge is about 2/3 as far as the origin, so the stated reason does not match the condition that triggers it.
excess: Level 4: 'The edge stores a response under a cache key, usually the URL plus selected headers. Cache-Control: max-age from the origin sets the TTL.' The reader knows HTTP caching headers, and the latency argument never uses this.

Level 4: 'Many CDNs route clients to the nearest edge with anycast or DNS steering.' A detour none of the questions use. Level 2 step 1 'DNS sends the client to a nearby edge server' is also a detour, since the limits card says DNS is left out of the model.
Summary item 1 repeats the lede ('A new HTTPS request needs 3 round trips… in proportion to distance') with nothing new.
The fact card 'Light in fiber is slower than in vacuum… about 1 ms per round trip' repeats the 1 ms/100 km rule already given in the predict section and Level 3.
Header eyebrow 'Explainer · Stage 3 · interactive'. The 'Stage 3' label means nothing to the reader.

gaps: The page never states when a miss becomes slower than no CDN. Q11 can only be answered by deriving it from the script; the visible text says only 'much closer' and 'not closer', and the second is wrong for the range between about 2/3 and 1 of the origin distance.
Miss and hit formulas are never written out. Only the no-CDN law is shown.

Geometry is inconsistent. The diagram puts the edge between client and origin (implying a client–origin distance of 6,300 km), but the model sets client–origin = edge–origin = 6,000 km. The reader is not told why.
The page does not explain why the edge–origin connection stays open while the client's does not, though the miss argument depends on it.
Default miss (90 ms) and hit (10 ms) totals appear only in the bars and the script, never in the text.
Summary item 2 says 'A faster origin would save only its 20 ms of processing'. This is never set up or used in the argument.

The case 'when a CDN helps little' (Q10) depends on an unexplained /3 threshold in the verdict code. The reader also has to combine it with the connection-reuse card, because the page never shows how much an already-open connection shrinks the gain.

reasons.11: The threshold (3×short + 1 > 2×long, so client–edge above about 2/3 of the origin distance) and the 2,000/1,000 km counterexample (91 vs 50 ms) are correct. But the inequality as written, '3×short + 21 > 3×long + 20', drops the long round trip from the miss time (miss = 3×short + long + 21), and it is not equivalent to the 'that is' form that follows. The answer also never states the expected main claim: in the normal case, with the edge much closer than the origin, a miss is still faster because it adds only one long round trip on an open connection. It gives no positive numeric case either, such as 90 vs 200 ms.

reasons.5: Calls the 1 ms per 100 km figure a fact. model.md marks it as an estimate that rests on the straight-path assumption; only the two-thirds speed of light in fiber is a fact. The answer also leaves out the stated simplifications (DNS, bandwidth and TLS session resumption are left out). The assumptions it does name (straight-line paths, client–origin about equal to edge–origin) are correct.
reasons.11: The threshold derivation is correct (a miss is slower when 3×short + 1 > 2×long), and so is the counterexample of a 91 ms miss against 50 ms. Two parts of the full answer are missing. It does not give the example of edge 300 km and origin 6,000 km, where a miss takes 90 ms against 200 ms. In the counterexample it does not give the 61 ms hit time, which is also slower than the 50 ms with no CDN.
